transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you too, Dr. Smith. Well, what brings me in is... I just keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and on one side of my face. I really noticed it after seeing myself in a bunch of recent family photos, and now I just can't stop focusing on it. 

My wife says she barely notices anything, and my clients at work don't seem to see it either, but... it's just really bothering me, so I figured I should talk to someone about it.
When you focus on this concern about your jaw, do you find yourself repeatedly checking it in the mirror or seeking constant reassurance from others?

Yeah, I definitely check it a lot. Like, before client meetings, I’ll usually go check the bathroom mirror, or I'll just use my phone camera several times. I find myself trying to adjust the lighting, or maybe change my collar, or just angle my face a certain way to see how it looks. 

And... I don't really ask for reassurance from others that much, but I do compare myself to other people constantly. I'll catch myself comparing my face to the younger advisors at the firm, or people at gallery events my wife and I go to, and I realize I'm doing that instead of actually focusing on the conversation I'm having.
Does this preoccupation with your jaw ever cause you to avoid social situations or delay getting your work done?

Well, I wouldn't say I completely avoid things, but it definitely has an impact. I still get all my work done, but... lately, I've been a bit slower getting out the door for client meetings because I'm caught up checking the mirror. And like I mentioned, sometimes I'm just less present during the actual appointments because I'm distracted by it. 

As for social stuff, my wife and I usually go to a lot of art openings, but I've actually skipped a few recently. I just... I didn't want to be seen, and I definitely didn't want to risk being photographed. So it does get in the way sometimes.
Beyond checking your reflection, do you find yourself engaging in repetitive behaviors like touching, measuring, or grooming the area around your jaw to try to improve its appearance?

No, I don't really do any of that. I mean, I might touch my face sometimes just out of habit, but I'm not measuring it or constantly rubbing it to try and fix it. And I don't spend hours grooming or anything like that. It's really just the mirror checking and the comparing that I do.
Have you ever sought out or considered any cosmetic procedures or treatments to address this concern about your jawline?

No, I haven't. I mean, I've never actually gone to a doctor or looked into surgery or injections or anything like that. I guess the thought has crossed my mind a couple of times when I'm feeling really frustrated with how it looks, but I've never taken any steps to actually do it. It just hasn't gotten to that point.

inference_history.note: The patient is presenting with a preoccupation with a perceived defect in physical appearance that others do not notice, which is the hallmark of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). I am also keeping Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) and Delusional Disorder, somatic type (F22) as differentials to rule out the severity and nature of the belief.

The patient's focus on a specific, minor, or non-existent physical flaw (jaw symmetry), combined with repetitive checking behaviors and social comparison, strongly points toward Body Dysmorphic Disorder. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) and Delusional Disorder (F22) are less likely given the specific nature of the preoccupation and the lack of broader delusional systems or generalized worry.
